Everything you strictly need for this course is on this site. What follows is
the short list of outside tools that are actually worth your time, with a note
on when each one helps.

::: {.callout-important}
## Several of these sites now have AI assistants built in

The course policy is unchanged and applies here too: **no AI use whatsoever**,
including chat panels and "explain this code" buttons embedded in otherwise
useful tools. Use the visualizer, the tutorial, and the reference. Do not use
the AI attached to them. See [Academic Honesty](../policies/honesty.qmd).

If a tool's non-AI parts stop being usable without the AI, tell me and I will
find a replacement.
:::

---

## See your code run: Python Tutor

[**pythontutor.com/cpp.html**](https://pythontutor.com/cpp.html)

Despite the name, it visualizes C++. You paste in a short program and step
through it one line at a time, watching variables appear, values change, and
**pointers drawn as actual arrows into actual memory cells**.

This is the single most useful tool on this page for the first half of the
semester. If a pointer, an array, or a linked list is not making sense, put
fifteen lines of it in here and step through. It is the same picture we build in
class, except you can run it at midnight.

Best used on **small** programs. Twenty lines with one confusing idea, not your
whole assignment.

---

## Learn it properly: LearnCpp

[**learncpp.com**](https://www.learncpp.com/)

A free, complete, genuinely well-written C++ tutorial. When a lecture moved too
fast, this is where to go for a slower, longer treatment with more examples. The
chapters below line up with what we have covered so far:

| If you want more on | Read |
|---|---|
| Uninitialized variables and undefined behaviour | [1.6](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/uninitialized-variables-and-undefined-behavior/) |
| `cout`, `cin`, `endl` | [1.5](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/introduction-to-iostream-cout-cin-and-endl/) |
| Data types and `sizeof` | [4.1](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/introduction-to-fundamental-data-types/), [4.3](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/object-sizes-and-the-sizeof-operator/) |
| Decimal, binary, hex, octal | [5.3](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/numeral-systems-decimal-binary-hexadecimal-and-octal/) |
| `const` | [5.1](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/constant-variables-named-constants/) |
| **Pointers, from the beginning** | [12.7](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/introduction-to-pointers/) |
| Arrays, and why `a[i]` is `*(a + i)` | [17.7](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/introduction-to-c-style-arrays/), [17.9](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/pointer-arithmetic-and-subscripting/) |
| The compiler, linker, and what `make` did | [0.5](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/introduction-to-the-compiler-linker-and-libraries/) |
| Debugging strategy | [3.3](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/a-strategy-for-debugging/) |

Each chapter ends with a quiz. Doing those quizzes is exactly the kind of
practice that makes a check-in go well.

---

## Look it up: cppreference

[**en.cppreference.com**](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp)

The authoritative C++ reference. It is precise, complete, and **written for
people who already know C++**, so it can feel cold at first. That is fine: use
it to answer narrow questions, not to learn from.

Good question for cppreference: *what exactly does `std::vector::resize` do when
the new size is smaller?*

Bad question for cppreference: *what is a vector?* Use LearnCpp for that.

Learning to read a language reference is itself a skill this course expects you
to pick up. Start now, in small doses.

---

## Bridge from Python: C++ for Python Programmers

[**Runestone: C++ for Python Programmers**](https://runestone.academy/runestone/books/published/cpp4python/index.html)

The reading already listed against the first weeks on the
[Schedule](schedule.qmd). Worth naming again here, because if you are fluent in
Python and keep tripping over C++ syntax, this is written for exactly that
situation.

---

::: {.callout-note}
## Nothing here replaces doing the work

These tools help you understand something you are stuck on. They do not
substitute for writing code yourself, which is the only thing that makes a
check-in go well. When in doubt, close the tab and try to write it from a blank
file, then come back.
:::

Found something genuinely useful that is not here? Send it to me and I will add
it.
